place.why: Address in London and mention of St Thomas' Hospital, which is a public hospital in England

summary: St Thomas’ is public NHS care run by Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust. For a complaint, the official England route is trust or commissioner first, normally within 12 months, then the Public Service Ombudsman if you are still unhappy; for compensation, this is a clinical negligence claim with a usual 3-year limit, handled against the trust with NHS Resolution meeting the costs under the NHS trust scheme. Free complaint help exists through PALS and NHS complaints advocacy, and to find a solicitor you can use the Law Society’s Find a Solicitor search for Clinical Negligence in London; the trust’s own complaint and records pages were found but blocked to the agent in this run, so some trust-specific form details could not be verified.

steps.body: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust / St Thomas' Hospital
steps.what: St Thomas' Hospital is public NHS hospital care run by Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust. For a formal NHS complaint about this hospital, England's rules say complain either to the hospital/trust or to the commissioner, not both, normally within 12 months; the trust's own complaint pages and online form were found but blocked to the agent by the trust site, so the trust-specific response time could not be verified in this run.
steps.deadline: "Complaints should normally be made within 12 months of an incident or of it coming to your attention."
steps.wall: bot_check on the trust site prevented reading the complaint page and form in this run
points: St Thomas' is listed on NHS as supplied by Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust.
For hospital care, you can complain to the provider directly or to the commissioner, but not both.
Complaints should normally be made within 12 months of the incident or of it coming to your attention.
When the complaint is acknowledged, the body must offer to discuss how it will be handled and the response period.
National rules require the response to be sent 'as soon as reasonably practicable' after investigation, not by a fixed national number of days.
The trust site refused the agent's browser on the complaint page and complaint form, so the trust's current form fields and response-time wording could not be captured here.
steps.appliesIf: NHS/public care at St Thomas' Hospital in England.
alternatives: Complain to the local integrated care board instead of the trust, but not both.
Use PALS first for help or early resolution.

sources.quote: Information supplied by Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust

Contact your local integrated care board (ICB) for complaints about primary care services (GPs, dentists, opticians or pharmacists) and secondary care, such as hospital care, mental health services, out-of-hours services, NHS 111 and community services like district nursing.

You can either complain to the NHS service provider directly (such as a GP, dentist surgery or hospital) or to the commissioner of the services, which is the body that pays for the NHS services you use. You cannot complain to both.
Complaints should normally be made within 12 months of an incident or of it coming to your attention.
At the time it acknowledges the complaint, the responsible body must offer to discuss with the complainant, at a time to be agreed with the complainant—
As soon as reasonably practicable after completing the investigation, the responsible body must send the complainant in writing a response, signed by the responsible person, which includes—

steps.what: If you are still unhappy after complaining to Guy's and St Thomas' or the commissioner first, the independent escalation route is the Public Service Ombudsman for NHS complaints in England. It uses a complaint checker which leads into the online complaint form; if you want payment as an outcome, the Ombudsman says you need to have explored legal action first and it cannot investigate where legal action was an option.
steps.deadline: "If you're still unhappy, complain to us within 12 months of knowing about the issue"
points: You must complain to the organisation first.
Complain to the Ombudsman within 12 months of knowing about the issue.
Use its complaint checker first.
The checker starts by asking what your complaint is about.
The Ombudsman says it has a three-step process.
If you want payment from the complaint route, you must first have explored legal action.
requires: If seeking payment from the complaint route, explore legal action first.
steps.appliesIf: You have already complained about NHS care in England and remain unhappy with the result or handling.
alternatives: Clinical negligence compensation claim through the courts/NHS Resolution.
Use the hospital complaint route first if you have not yet done so.
missing: Whether the trust has sent its complaint response yet.

sources.quote: Complain to the organisation you're unhappy with first
If you're still unhappy, complain to us within 12 months of knowing about the issue
Use our complaint checker to see if we can help.
To start with, please tell us what is your complaint about?
We have a three-step process for dealing with complaints.
If you are looking for payment as an outcome from your complaint then you will need to have explored the option of taking legal action before you come to us.

steps.body: NHS Resolution / Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts / courts of England and Wales
steps.what: For harm from NHS care at St Thomas' Hospital, compensation is by a clinical negligence claim, usually settled or litigated under the courts of England and Wales, not by a no-fault scheme. Guy's and St Thomas' remains the legal defendant, but NHS Resolution handles the claim and pays the associated costs through the Clinical Negligence Scheme for Trusts because all NHS Trusts and Foundation Trusts in England belong to it.
steps.deadline: "Compensation claims for personal injury are subject to a ‘limitation period’ of three years."
points: To get compensation, the claimant must prove both breach of duty and causation.
If acting without a lawyer, NHS Resolution says to send a 'letter of claim' to the NHS Trust responsible for the care.
Personal injury clinical negligence claims are subject to a three-year limitation period.
All NHS Trusts, including Foundation Trusts, in England currently belong to CNST.
When a claim is made, the NHS body remains the legal defendant but NHS Resolution handles the claim and meets the associated costs.
NHS Resolution also uses mediation and other dispute resolution methods to avoid unnecessary court proceedings where possible.
steps.appliesIf: You seek money for harm caused by allegedly negligent NHS treatment at St Thomas' Hospital.
alternatives: NHS complaints procedure to get explanations before or alongside considering a claim.
Mediation or other NHS Resolution dispute resolution methods during a claim.
missing: Exact date of knowledge for limitation purposes if argued later.
Whether any limitation exception could apply, such as lack of capacity.

sources.quote: To receive compensation, you will need to show both ‘breach of duty of care’ and ‘causation’ has taken place.

If you do not have legal representation and you plan on representing yourself in court as a litigant in person, you will need to submit what is called a ‘letter of claim’ to the NHS Trust that was responsible for your care.
Compensation claims for personal injury are subject to a ‘limitation period’ of three years.
Although membership of the scheme is voluntary, all NHS Trusts (including Foundation Trusts) in England currently belong to the scheme.
When a claim is made against a member of CNST, the NHS body remains the legal defendant.
However, we take over full responsibility for handling the claim and meeting the associated costs.

steps.body: Legal Aid Agency / Ministry of Justice / NHS Resolution
steps.what: For an adult clinical negligence claim like this in England, ordinary civil legal aid is generally not available. The main funding route is usually a conditional fee agreement ('no win, no fee'); for personal injury claims, the success fee taken from damages is capped by law.
points: Civil legal aid for clinical negligence remains in scope only for a neurological injury causing severe disability to a child around birth, not for a standard adult fracture-misdiagnosis claim.
The official legal aid adviser finder says advisers will ask about your problem and finances to work out eligibility.
The official search route is by postcode for clinical negligence advisers in England and Wales.
In personal injury claims, success fees are capped at 25% of specified damages and not future pecuniary loss.
The 25% cap applies at first instance.
NHS Resolution's complaints/claim pages do not offer a no-fault redress funding scheme for this kind of case.
steps.appliesIf: Clinical negligence claim in England and Wales; this patient's story is an adult NHS hospital claim.
alternatives: Conditional fee agreement with a clinical negligence solicitor.
Privately funded claim or self-representation, though NHS Resolution gives a letter-of-claim template for litigants in person.
missing: Whether the patient has already spoken to any legal aid provider.
Whether any unusual exception could apply, such as lack of capacity or another separate legal issue in scope.

sources.quote: “Civil legal services provided in relation to a claim for damages in respect of clinical negligence which caused a neurological injury to an individual (“V”) as a result of which V is severely disabled, but only where the first and second conditions are met.”
“while V was in his or her mother's womb, or”
Search for official legal aid advisers in England and Wales.
When you contact the adviser they'll ask about your problem and finances to work out if you can get legal aid.

Article 5 provides that, in a claim for personal injuries, the success fee shall be limited to a maximum of 25% of the damages awarded for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and pecuniary loss, other than future pecuniary loss and net of any sums recoverable by the Compensation Recovery Unit, inclusive of VAT.
Article 5 further limits the effect of the 25% cap to proceedings at first instance.

steps.body: The Law Society of England and Wales
steps.what: To find a clinical negligence solicitor for a St Thomas' claim, use the Law Society's official Find a Solicitor directory. It lets you search by legal issue and location, such as Clinical Negligence and London or your postcode.
points: The Law Society says Find a Solicitor helps you find a solicitor who offers the services you need.
Its help page says quick search lets you search by legal issue and location.
You can enter a postcode, town, city or country.
The official directory also offers quick search and advanced search.
steps.appliesIf: You want a solicitor regulated in England and Wales for a clinical negligence case.

steps.body: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
steps.what: The national body that publishes the core health and care guidance used by NHS services in England is NICE. Its guidance is not a hospital complaint route, but it is the main official source to check the clinical guidance doctors are expected to use alongside specialist and local guidance.
points: NICE says it produces guidance for the NHS and wider health and care system.
Its guidance includes clinical guidelines and other evidence-based product types.
steps.appliesIf: Clinical guidance question for NHS care in England.

sources.quote: We produce useful and usable guidance for the NHS and wider health and care system.

Our guidance takes many forms: NICE guidelines (clinical, social care, public health, medicines practice), technology appraisals, interventional procedures, medical technologies, diagnostics and highly specialised technologies.

steps.body: NHS complaints advocacy / Healthwatch / NHS PALS
steps.what: Free help exists before or during an NHS complaint. NHS England says you can use PALS at most hospitals, and if you are making or thinking about making a complaint you can get free help from an NHS complaints advocate; advocates are independent of the NHS.
points: NHS England says PALS is a free service in most hospitals.
NHS England says you can get free help from an NHS complaints advocate.
It tells patients to search for local NHS complaints advocacy or ask local Healthwatch.
The NHS advocacy page says advocates are there to help people speak up and can support complaints.
The NHS service-directory page for St Thomas' lists PALS with phone 020 7188 8801.
steps.appliesIf: You want help understanding or making an NHS complaint in England.
alternatives: Use a local independent advocate found through your council or advocacy organisation.
Use Healthwatch to find the local advocacy provider.

sources.quote: The Patient Advice and Liaison Service (PALS) is a free, confidential and independent service that you’ll find in most hospitals.
If you’re making, or thinking about making, a complaint, you could get free help from an NHS complaints advocate.
Search online for ‘NHS complaints advocacy’ in your area or contact your local Healthwatch to find out who provides NHS complaints advocacy in your area.
Advocates make sure you're heard.

In this run, the trust's records page and MyChart route were found but blocked to the agent, so the trust-specific form details could not be verified; NHS England's official fallback says to contact the relevant hospital trust's records manager or patient services manager.
